common_name: Li'l Bang Daybreak Coreopsis (Dwarf Disease-Resistant Bicolor Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Daybreak is a dwarf sibling of the Big Bang coreopsis series bred by Darrell Probst, noted for strong disease resistance and a compact habit well suited to small beds and containers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Daybreak is a compact coreopsis from the Li'l Bang series, a dwarf line bred from the disease-resistant Big Bang parentage, producing bright orange-red and yellow bicolor flowers over a dense, tidy mound. Its small size and disease resistance make it a strong choice for the front of a border, edging, or a sunny container where a taller coreopsis would be out of scale. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall and tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established. Shear the plant back lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.
sources: Proven Winners — US Plant Patent PP27138

common_name: Li'l Bang Starstruck Coreopsis (Dwarf Rosy-Pink Disease-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Starstruck is a dwarf, rosy-pink-flowered member of the disease-resistant Li'l Bang coreopsis series, a compact size well suited to small Gulf Coast beds and containers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Starstruck is a compact coreopsis from the Li'l Bang series, standing out for its unusual rosy-pink flower color among a genus more often known for yellow and orange tones, held over a dense, tidy mound of fine foliage. It shares the series' strong disease resistance and blooms heavily from early summer into fall, tolerating heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established. Its small stature makes it a good fit for the front of a border, edging, or a sunny container. Shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.
sources: Proven Winners — US Plant Patent PP28006

common_name: Pardon My Purple Bee Balm (Extremely Compact Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pardon My Purple is an extremely compact bee balm bred with good resistance to the powdery mildew that plagues taller, older Monarda cultivars in humid Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Pardon My Purple is a compact bee balm cultivar, standing barely a foot tall, bred with notably better powdery mildew resistance than many older, taller Monarda varieties that often defoliate badly by midsummer in humid conditions. It produces the classic shaggy, tubular purple flowers beloved by hummingbirds and bees, on a tidy mound scaled for a smaller border or container rather than the back of a bed. Good air circulation, achieved through adequate spacing, further reduces mildew pressure. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding.

common_name: Pardon My Cerise Bee Balm (Compact Cherry-Pink Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pardon My Cerise is a compact bee balm bred with better-than-average powdery mildew resistance, a real advantage for a Gulf South summer where mildew often defoliates older Monarda varieties.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Pardon My Cerise is a compact bee balm bearing dark cherry-pink, shaggy tubular flowers on an eighteen-inch plant, considerably shorter than heirloom bee balm types and bred with better-than-average resistance to the powdery mildew that commonly defoliates taller Monarda varieties in humid summer weather. Its bright flowers draw hummingbirds and butterflies through the summer, and the compact size fits more easily into a mixed perennial border than older, sprawling bee balm cultivars. Provide good air circulation with adequate spacing to further reduce mildew pressure. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Balmy Pink Bee Balm (Dwarf Non-Flopping Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Balmy Pink is a dwarf bee balm bred with sturdy, non-flopping stems and good powdery mildew resistance, a compact, tidy option for a Gulf South pollinator border.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Balmy Pink is a dwarf bee balm cultivar noted for sturdy, upright stems that resist the flopping common in taller Monarda varieties, along with good resistance to the powdery mildew that often disfigures bee balm foliage in humid summer conditions. It bears the classic shaggy, tubular pink flowers over a compact, tidy mound that suits a smaller border or container planting. Its dwarf habit and disease resistance make it easier to keep looking attractive through a full Gulf South growing season than many heirloom bee balm types. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and provide good air circulation to further reduce mildew pressure.
